spec.title: Do CVs with white-sounding names get more callbacks? Bertrand and Mullainathan found 1.5 times as many
spec.statement: Bertrand and Mullainathan (American Economic Review, 2004) sent about 5,000 made-up CVs to real job ads in Boston and Chicago, giving them either white-sounding or Black-sounding names at random. CVs with white-sounding names got 1.50 times as many callbacks. This runs our own small program on a public copy of the experiment's data. The working paper's table has slightly more CVs than this data. The rebuild isn't the authors' code, so a mismatch ends as inconclusive.

source.license: Rebuild: MIT. Data: GPL-3 (OpenIntro), fetched from OpenIntro, not redistributed.
source.authors: M. Bertrand, S. Mullainathan; rebuild by the RERUN project

artifact.entrypoint: python names-on-cvs-2004/rebuild.py resume.csv > rerun_output.txt && cat rerun_output.txt

metric.name: callbacks for white-sounding names per callback for Black-sounding names

published_output_check: Table 1 of NBER 9873: 10.06% and 6.70% on 2,445 CVs per group, ratio 1.50. The public data has 2,435 per group: 9.65%, 6.45%, ratio 1.4968.
